The muon is discovered by Seth Neddermeyer and Carl D. Anderson at California Institute of Technology.
First publication recognizing stress as a biological condition.
Publication in the United Kingdom of Dr A. J. Cronin's novel The Citadel, promoting the cause of socialised medicine.
Konrad Zuse submits patents in Germany based on his Z1 computer design anticipating von Neumann architecture.
First total solar eclipse to exceed 7 minutes of totality in over 800 years; visible in the Pacific and Peru.
Carlo Perrier and Emilio Segrè at the University of Palermo confirm discovery of the chemical element which will become known as Technetium.
English chemist Montague Phillips at May & Baker synthesises sulphapyridine (M&B 693), an early antibiotic which immediately enters animal trials with Middlesex Hospital pathologist Lionel Whitby.
Otto Bayer and his coworkers at IG Farben in Leverkusen, Germany, first make polyurethanes.
Eugene Wigner introduces the term isospin.
Frank Whittle ground-tests the first jet engine designed to power an aircraft, at Rugby, England.
Albert Einstein and Nathan Rosen publish a paper denying that gravitational waves can exist.
The citric acid cycle is finally identified by Hans Adolf Krebs.
Robert Edward Gross becomes the first surgeon successfully to ligate an uninfected patent ductus arteriosus, in Boston.
Bawden and Pirie publish the first crystal of a spherical virus, Tomato bushy stunt virus.
Alan Turing completes his Ph.D. thesis, Systems of Logic Based on Ordinals, at Princeton University; it is presented to the London Mathematical Society on June 16.
Herbert E. Ives and G. R. Stilwell execute the Ives–Stilwell experiment, showing that ions radiate at frequencies affected by their motion.
The Vlasov equation is first proposed for description of plasma by Anatoly Vlasov.
Lysergic acid diethylamide is first synthesized by Albert Hofmann from ergotamine at the Sandoz Laboratories in Basel.
Hans Asperger first adopts the term autism in its modern sense in referring to autistic psychopaths in a lecture (in German) on child psychology.
A 450-ton meteorite strikes the Earth in an empty field near Chicora, Pennsylvania, United States.
Discovery of nuclear fission by Otto Hahn, Lise Meitner and Fritz Strassmann with Otto Robert Frisch.
László Bíró obtains his first patent for a ballpoint pen, in France.
The Einstein–Szilard letter is signed by Albert Einstein, advising President of the United States Franklin D. Roosevelt of the potential use of uranium to construct an atomic bomb.
With Hartland Snyder, he predicts the existence of what will come to be called black holes.
Alan Turing and Gordon Welchman report to the United Kingdom Government Code and Cypher School, Bletchley Park.
Sonderaktion Krakau: The Gestapo arrests scientists from the Jagiellonian University and other institutions in Kraków, Poland; on November 27 they are sent to Sachsenhausen concentration camp.
February – Discovery of nuclear fission is announced independently by Otto Hahn and Lise Meitner.
First meeting of the Advisory Committee on Uranium under Lyman James Briggs, authorised by President Roosevelt to oversee neutron experiments.
Richard von Mises poses the birthday problem in probability.
Flying the Heinkel He 178, Erich Warsitz makes the first flight entirely on turbojet power (the HeS 3 jet engine), at Rostock in Germany.
John H. Lawrence uses beams of energized neutrons from a particle accelerator to treat a patient with leukemia.
With George Volkoff, he calculates the structure of neutron stars.
The radioactive element Astatine is synthesized by Dale R. Corson, Kenneth Ross MacKenzie and Emilio Segrè at the University of California, Berkeley.
August – Alan Turing and Gordon Welchman at the United Kingdom Government Code and Cypher School, Bletchley Park, design the British Bombes to help decrypt Wehrmacht Enigma machine signals.
Plutonium is first synthesized by a team led by Glenn T. Seaborg and Edwin McMillan at the University of California, Berkeley by bombarding uranium-238 with deuterons.
Neptunium, the first transuranic element, is synthesized by Edwin McMillan and Philip H. Abelson at the University of California, Berkeley.
The antibiotic dactinomycin (actinomycin D) is first isolated by Selman Waksman and H. Boyd Woodruff at Rutgers University.
First free flight of Igor Sikorsky's Vought-Sikorsky VS-300 helicopter, in the United States.
The radioactive isotope carbon-14 is discovered by Martin Kamen and Sam Ruben at the University of California, Berkeley.
Ed Ricketts, John Steinbeck and six others leave Monterey for the Gulf of California on a marine invertebrate collecting expedition.
Women's stockings made of nylon are first placed on sale across the United States.
American Bantam deliver the first prototype BRC Quarter-Ton General Purpose Vehicle – the four-wheel drive Jeep, designed by Karl Probst.
Artificial nuclear transmutation of mercury into gold by fast neutrons is reported in Physical Review.
President of the United States Franklin D. Roosevelt signs Executive Order 8807 creating the Office of Scientific Research and Development with Vannevar Bush as its director.
German mineralogist Karl Hugo Strunz's Mineralogische Tabellen introduces Nickel–Strunz classification of minerals.
The first polyester fibre, polyethylene terephthalate (terylene), is patented by John Rex Whinfield, James T. Dickson and their employer the Calico Printers' Association of Manchester, England.
Chemical element 94, plutonium, is first synthesized by Glenn T. Seaborg, Arthur C. Wahl, Joseph W. Kennedy and Emilio Segrè.
Birmingham Accident Hospital opens as the world's first trauma centre in Birmingham, England.

Reserve Constable Albert Alexander, a sepsis patient at the Radcliffe Infirmary in Oxford, becomes the first person treated with penicillin intravenously, by Howard Florey's team, injected by Dr Charles Fletcher.
Folic acid is first isolated via extraction from spinach leaves by Herschel K. Mitchell, Esmond E. Snell and Roger J. Williams at the University of Texas at Austin.
German engineer Konrad Zuse presents the Z3, the world's first working programmable, Turing complete, fully automatic computer, to an audience of aviation engineers in Berlin.
Prototype AI Mk. VIII radar, the first operational microwave-frequency aircraft interception (AI) radar, introduced by the British Royal Air Force.

The first V-2 rocket is successfully launched from Test Stand VII at Peenemünde, Germany, flying a distance of 147 km and reaching a height of 84.5 km, becoming the first man-made object to reach space.
James Stanley Hey, a British Army research officer, first detects radio waves emitted by the Sun, helping to pioneer radio astronomy.
First operational military Bailey bridge erected by British Royal Engineers over the Medjerda River near Majaz al Bab in Tunisia.
Alfred Gilman, Louis S. Goodman and Frederick S. Philips first carry out trials of anti-cancer chemotherapy, using mechlorethamine.
John V. Atanasoff with Clifford Berry successfully test the Atanasoff–Berry Computer, the first electronic digital computing device.

Chicago Pile-1, the first nuclear reactor, goes critical under the squash court of the University of Chicago, thanks to the efforts of Enrico Fermi, Leó Szilárd, George Weil and the rest of the Chicago pile team.
Isaac Asimov's Three Laws of Robotics are introduced in his short story "Runaround" published in Astounding Science-Fiction.
German pathologist Max Westenhöfer first puts forward an aquatic ape hypothesis.

Composer George Antheil and actress Hedy Lamarr are granted a United States patent for a frequency-hopping spread spectrum communication system intended to make radio-guided torpedoes harder to detect.
Walter Bruch operates a closed-circuit television system to monitor the V-2 rocket launches.
Abraham Maslow proposes the Hierarchy of Needs theory of psychology in his paper "A Theory of Human Motivation".
The cinder cone volcano Parícutin begins to appear in Mexico, giving volcanologists an unusual opportunity to observe its complete life cycle.
Winston Churchill's recurring bacterial pneumonia is successfully treated with the sulphapyridine M&B 693, a first-generation sulphonamide antibiotic.
The University of Oxford acquires the nearby Wytham Woods which become an important centre for research into ecology in England.
The antibiotic streptomycin (the first antibiotic remedy for tuberculosis) is first isolated by Albert Schatz in the laboratory of Selman Abraham Waksman at Rutgers University in the United States.
Lyle Goodhue and William Sullivan patent the refillable aerosol spray in the United States, for use with mosquito–repellant.
Leo Kanner of the Johns Hopkins Hospital first publicly adopts the term autism in its modern sense in English in referring to early infantile autism and describes "Patient No. 1", Donald Triplett.
Living specimens of Metasequoia glyptostroboides, the Dawn Redwood, previously known only as a Mesozoic fossil, are located in China.
A golden mould, Penicillium chrysogenum, growing on an American cantaloupe in Peoria, Illinois, is found to be ideal for mass production of penicillin.
Krueger flaps for aircraft wings are invented by Werner Krüger and evaluated in the wind tunnels in Göttingen.
Last known evidence for existence of the Asiatic lion in the wild in Iran (Khuzestan province).
Hendrik van de Hulst predicts the 21 cm hyperfine line of neutral interstellar hydrogen.
Hanford Site in Washington (state) produces its first plutonium.
Donald Griffin with G. W. Pierce demonstrate that bats use high-frequency sound in a technique which Griffin describes as echolocation.
Erwin Schrödinger publishes What is Life?, containing conceptual discussion of the genetic code and of negentropy.
Americium discovered by Glenn T. Seaborg, et al.
First operational use of a snorkel on a submarine.
The Whipple Museum of the History of Science is established when Robert Whipple presents his collection of scientific instruments to the University of Cambridge, England.
Group Captain James Stagg correctly forecasts a brief improvement in weather conditions over the English Channel which permits the following day's Normandy landings to take place.
IBM dedicates the first program-controlled calculator, the Automatic Sequence Controlled Calculator, best known as the Harvard Mark I.
The Bachem Ba 349 Natter is launched from Stetten am kalten Markt.
A team at Oak Ridge National Laboratory led by Charles Coryell discovers chemical element 61, the only one still missing between 1 and 96 on the periodic table, which they will name promethium.
Slinky toy first demonstrated by engineer Richard T. James in Philadelphia.
Salvador Edward Luria and Alfred Day Hershey independently recognize that viruses undergo mutations.
Nuclear testing: the Trinity test, the first test of an atomic bomb, using 6 kilograms of plutonium, succeeds in detonating an explosion equivalent to that of 20 kilotons of TNT.
Dorothy Hodgkin and C. H. (Harry) Carlisle publish the first three-dimensional molecular structure of a steroid, cholesteryl iodide.
Arthur C. Clarke puts forward the idea of a geosynchronous communications satellite.
Atomic bombings of Hiroshima and Nagasaki make the world aware of the power of nuclear weapons.
Kathleen Lonsdale and Marjory Stephenson become the first women elected as Fellows of the Royal Society of London.
The first desalination plant becomes operational.
Peter Scott opens the Slimbridge Wetland Reserve in England.
Dr. Benjamin Spock's The Common Sense Book of Baby and Child Care is first published in New York; it becomes one of the biggest best-sellers of all time.
Alfred Gilman, with Frederick S. Philips, first publish the results of trials of anti-cancer chemotherapy, using mechlorethamine, carried out with Louis S. Goodman.
Reginald Aldworth Daly of Harvard University first proposes a giant impact hypothesis to account for formation of the Moon.
Frederic Calland Williams receives a patent for a random-access memory device.
The United States Army Signal Corps' Project Diana bounces radar waves off the Moon.
Atomic Energy Research Establishment established at Harwell, Oxfordshire under John Cockcroft.
The Blanuša snarks (two snarks with 18 vertices) are discovered in graph theory by Danilo Blanuša.
Edmund Jaeger discovers and later documents, in The Condor, a state of extended torpor, approaching hibernation, in a bird, the common poorwill.
Summer – Ottenby Bird Observatory begins to function on the Swedish island of Öland.
Zika virus first isolated from a rhesus macaque in the Zika Forest of Uganda.
First recorded use of the word computer in its modern sense, referring to an electronic digital machine.
The Shelter Island Conference on the Foundations of Quantum Mechanics convenes in New York State.
Mary Barber publishes her classic paper on antibiotic resistance in Staphylococcus bacteria.
Sikhote-Alin meteorite falls to Earth in Siberia, the largest iron meteorite known to have impacted.

'GLEEP' (the Graphite Low Energy Experimental Pile) experimental nuclear reactor runs for the first time at the Atomic Energy Research Establishment, Harwell, Oxfordshire, the first reactor to operate in Western Europe.
The Oxford Swift Research Project, based on the colony at the Oxford University Museum of Natural History, is started by David and Elizabeth Lack.
December 23 – John Bardeen and Walter Brattain working under William Shockley at AT&T's Bell Labs in the United States demonstrate the transistor effect.
The International Organization for Standardization (ISO) is founded.
A moth lodged in a relay is found to be the cause of a malfunction in the Harvard Mark II electromechanical computer, logged as "First actual case of bug being found.".
The World Health Organization is established by the United Nations.
Last recorded sighting of the Caspian tiger in Kazakhstan.
In psychology, Bertram Forer demonstrates the Barnum effect (that people tend to accept generalised descriptions of personality as uniquely applicable to themselves).
Physicists Ralph Asher Alpher and George Gamow publish the Alpher–Bethe–Gamow paper about the Big Bang.
First modern long-span permanent box girder bridge completed, between Cologne and Deutz.
Teaching and research in Mendelian genetics is prohibited in the Soviet Union in favour of Lysenkoist theories of the inheritance of acquired characteristics.
Delegates to a conference organised by Sir Julian Huxley at Fontainebleau agree to formation of the International Union for Conservation of Nature.
World's first working program run on an electronic stored-program computer, the Manchester Baby (written by Tom Kilburn).

October – Claude E. Shannon publishes "A Mathematical Theory of Communication" in Bell System Technical Journal, regarded as a foundation of information theory, introducing the concept of Shannon entropy and adopting the term Bit.
The South Island takahē, a flightless bird generally thought to have been extinct for fifty years, is rediscovered by Geoffrey Orbell near Lake Te Anau in the South Island of New Zealand.
Ambato earthquake in Ecuador, measuring 6.8 on the Richter magnitude scale.
Los Angeles receives its first recorded snowfall.
EDSAC, the first practicable stored-program computer, runs its first program at University of Cambridge in England, to calculate a table of squares.
The Lanczos tensor is introduced in general relativity by Cornelius Lanczos.
A group including Dorothy Hodgkin publish the three-dimensional molecular structure of penicillin, demonstrating that it contains a β-lactam ring.
Gilbert Ryle's book The Concept of Mind, a founding document in the philosophy of mind, is published.
The Hale Telescope at Palomar Observatory in California, the largest aperture optical telescope in the world for 28 years, sees first light.
Freeman Dyson demonstrates the equivalence of the formulations of quantum electrodynamics existing at this time, incidentally inventing the Dyson series.
J. B. S. Haldane proposes the Darwin as a unit of evolutionary change.
The use of lithium salts to control mania is rediscovered by Australian psychiatrist John Cade, the first mood stabilizer.
Dutch astronomer Jan Oort postulates the existence of an orbiting cloud of planets (the Oort cloud) at the outermost edge of the Solar System.
Publication of Alan Turing's paper "Computing Machinery and Intelligence", seminal in the study of artificial intelligence and presenting the Turing test.
In his encyclical Humani generis, Pope Pius XII declares evolution to be a serious hypothesis that does not contradict essential Roman Catholic teachings.
Melvin Calvin, James Bassham, and Andrew Benson at the University of California, Berkeley, discover the Calvin cycle in photosynthesis.
Enrico Fermi discusses the Fermi paradox.
Entomologist Willi Hennig publishes Grundzüge einer Theorie der phylogenetischen Systematik in East Germany, pioneering the study of cladistics.
Full-scale release of myxomatosis for control of the Australian rabbit population.

Californium, a radioactive actinide transuranium element, is first synthesized by Stanley G. Thompson, Kenneth Street Jr., Albert Ghiorso and Glenn T. Seaborg at the University of California, Berkeley.

A field-sequential color system developed by Hungarian American engineer Dr. Peter Goldmark becomes the first color television system to be adopted for commercial use (by CBS in the United States), but is abandoned a year later.
Canadians Harry Wasylyk, Larry Hansen and Frank Plomp introduce the plastic bin bag for garbage collection.
The progestin norethisterone, significant in creation of the combined oral contraceptive pill, is synthesized by Carl Djerassi, Luis E. Miramontes and George Rosenkranz at Syntex in Mexico City.
Operation Greenhouse: The first thermonuclear weapon, developed by Edward Teller and Stanislaw Ulam, is tested in the "George" test on Enewetok Atoll in the Marshall Islands by the United States.
The World Health Organization's report on maternal deprivation, Maternal Care and Mental Health, written by English psychologist John Bowlby, is published.
The continental United States becomes malaria-free.
Karl Huber's biography of Leibniz is published posthumously.
EDVAC binary electronic stored program computer incorporating high speed delay-line memory begins operation at the United States Army's Ballistics Research Laboratory at Aberdeen Proving Ground.
Indian Institute of Technology Kharagpur inaugurated in West Bengal as the first of the Indian Institutes of Technology.
William Shockley of Bell Labs in the United States announces the invention jointly with John Bardeen and Walter Brattain of the grown-junction transistor.
Remington Rand delivers the first UNIVAC I computer to the United States Census Bureau.
Niko Tinbergen publishes The Study of Instinct.
Last confirmed sighting of the Caribbean monk seal, at Serranilla Bank, between Jamaica and Nicaragua.
The first successful sex reassignment surgery is performed in Copenhagen, making George Jorgensen Jr. become Christine Jorgensen.
The first successful surgical separation of conjoined twins is conducted in Mount Sinai Hospital, Cleveland, Ohio.
Alan Turing's paper "The Chemical Basis of Morphogenesis" is published, putting forward a reaction–diffusion hypothesis of pattern formation, considered a seminal piece of work in morphogenesis.
The first autocode and its compiler are developed by Alick Glennie for the Manchester Mark 1 computer, considered as the first working high-level compiled programming language.
Discovery by Derek J. de Solla Price of a lost medieval scientific work entitled Equatorie of the Planetis, initially attributed to Geoffrey Chaucer.
American obstetrical anesthesiologist Dr. Virginia Apgar devises the Apgar score as a simple replicable method of quickly and summarily assessing the health of babies immediately after childbirth.
Alan Hodgkin and Andrew Huxley publish the Hodgkin–Huxley model of action potentials in neurons of the squid giant axon.
Geoffrey Dummer proposes the integrated circuit.
John Forbes Nash Jr. produces groundbreaking work in the area of real algebraic geometry.

Physicians at the University of Rochester, New York, use frontal lobe novocaine injections to relieve cancer pain, inspired by Dr. van Wagenen’s psychiatric trials predicting lobotomy success; 60% respond well and undergo surgery.

Alan Turing publishes an article describing the first 1,104 zeroes of the Riemann zeta-function, the culmination of fifteen years of work on how to use computers to tackle a fundamental problem in number theory.

Enrico Fermi, John Pasta, Stanislaw Ulam, and Mary Tsingou conduct computer simulations of a vibrating string that included a non-linear term in what became known as the Fermi–Pasta–Ulam–Tsingou experiment.
American scientist Winston Price isolates the first rhinovirus, the most prevalent cause of the common cold.
Tom Kilburn at the University of Manchester completes a device called MEG, which performs floating-point calculations.
Jonas Salk announces his polio vaccine.
Cincinnati psychiatrist Max Lurie and Harry Salzer coin the term antidepressant.
Maurice Ewing and Bruce Heezen discover the deep canyon running along the center of the Mid-Atlantic Ridge, an important contribution to the theory of plate tectonics.
Linus Pauling proposes a DNA triple helix structure, which is rapidly shown to be incorrect.
The Jet Propulsion Laboratory completes development of the SSM-A-17 Corporal I rocket.
Last confirmed specimen of a Caspian tiger is killed, in the valley of the Sumbar River in the Kopet Dag Mountains of Turkmenistan.
The first specimens of the mineral benstonite are collected by Orlando J. Benston in the Magnet Cove igneous complex of Arkansas.
Daniel I. Arnon demonstrates in the laboratory the chemical function of photosynthesis in chloroplasts.
Texas Instruments announces development of the first commercial transistor radio, the Regency TR-1, manufactured in Indianapolis; it goes on sale the following month.
Heinz Sielmann makes the pioneering nature documentary about woodpeckers, Zimmerleute des Waldes ("Carpenters of the forest").
The first mass vaccination of children against polio begins, in Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania.
Staley T. McBrayer invents the Vanguard web offset press for newspaper printing in Fort Worth, Texas.
British epidemiologist Richard Doll submits a study on the risk to workers in asbestos manufacture of mortality from lung cancer.
Eduard Paul Tratz and Heinz Heck propose the species name bonobo for what was previously known as the pygmy chimpanzee.
Harold Hopkins and Narinder Singh Kapany at Imperial College London report achieving low-loss light transmission through a 75 cm long optical fiber bundle.
Erwin Müller and Kanwar Bahadur are the first people to observe individual atoms, using Müller's field ion microscope.
American geophysicist Clair Cameron Patterson presents his result for the age of the Earth using lead isotopic data from the Canyon Diablo meteorite – 4.55 billion years (± 70 million).

Heinz Fraenkel-Conrat shows that a virus consists of an infective RNA core and a non-infective protein coat; and with Robley C. Williams assembles a functional tobacco mosaic virus from purified versions of these components.
Total solar eclipse of 7 min 8 sec duration, the longest between the 11th and 22nd centuries, visible in Southeast Asia.
Enrico Fermi, John Pasta, Stanisław Ulam and Mary Tsingou numerically study a nonlinear spring model of heat conduction and discover solitary wave type behavior.
Severo Ochoa develops enzymes that cause nucleic acid bases to form RNA.

Mendelevium (atomic number 101) is first synthesized by Albert Ghiorso, Glenn T. Seaborg, Gregory R. Choppin, Bernard G. Harvey, and Stanley G. Thompson (team leader) at the University of California, Berkeley.
James F. Bonner and Paul Ts'o isolate mitochondria from cells.
First reported mitral valve replacement, by Judson Chesterman of Sheffield (England).
Former Luftwaffe flying ace Ulrich Steinhilper, a German IBM typewriter salesman, coins and popularizes the term "Textverarbeitung" ("word processing").
First Chamberlin electro-mechanical keyboard instrument, developed and patented by Wisconsin inventor Harry Chamberlin, is introduced.
TX-0 transistorized computer completed at MIT Lincoln Laboratory in the United States.
The hard disk drive is invented by an IBM team led by Reynold B. Johnson.
Calder Hall nuclear power station in England is first connected to the National Grid.
DIDO heavy water enriched uranium nuclear reactor opens at the Atomic Energy Research Establishment, Harwell, Oxfordshire, England.
Existence of the antineutron is experimentally confirmed by University of California, Berkeley physicist Bruce Cork.
First flight of Convair B-58, the first supersonic jet bomber capable of Mach 2 flight, designed by Robert H. Widmer.
Capri Bird Observatory is established on Capri.
Cooper pairs are first described by Leon Cooper.
General Electric/Telechron introduces model 7H241 "The Snooz Alarm", first snooze alarm clock.
National Polytechnical Museum established in Sofia, Bulgaria.
Reactor goes critical in Shippingport Atomic Power Station, Pennsylvania, the first commercial pressurized water reactor.
IBM delivers the first compiler for the FORTRAN scientific programming language.
Karl Prachar publishes a key text on the distribution of prime numbers, Primzahlverteilung.
A report by the Medical Research Council (UK) reveals evidence to support a link between tobacco smoking and lung cancer.
Launch of Sputnik 1, the first artificial satellite, by an R-7 Semyorka rocket from the Baikonur Cosmodrome near Tyuratam in the Kazakh Soviet Socialist Republic.
BCS theory of superconductivity developed by John Bardeen, Leon Cooper, and Robert Schrieffer.
Dopamine is first identified in the human brain by Katharine Montagu.
Launch of Sputnik 2, with a dog called Laika on board, the first animal sent into orbit.
Rudolf Mössbauer discovers the Mössbauer effect.
The 3rd Soviet Antarctic Expedition discovers the subglacial Gamburtsev Mountain Range in Antarctica; also becoming the first to reach the Southern Pole of Inaccessibility (December 14).

Denatonium, the bitterest chemical compound known (used as an aversive agent), is discovered during research on local anesthetics by Macfarlan Smith of Edinburgh, Scotland, and registered under the trademark Bitrex.
John McCarthy specifies the Lisp programming language.
The first successful American satellite, Explorer I, is launched into orbit.
Arthur L. Schawlow and Charles H. Townes of Bell Laboratories publish a paper in Physical Review Letters setting out the principles of the optical laser.
The United States Congress formally creates the National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA).
Friedrich L. Bauer and other members of the ZMMD-Group build a working ALGOL 58 compiler.
Jack Kilby demonstrates the first integrated circuit.
Anne McLaren, with John D. Biggers, reports the first mammals, a litter of mice, grown from embryos developed in vitro and transferred to a surrogate mother.
Francis Crick states the "central dogma of molecular biology".
The Caspian tiger becomes extinct in Iran.
Yardymli meteorite makes a landfall in Azerbaijan.
The Japanese medical research group studying Minamata disease comes to the conclusion that mercury is the cause.
The specification for the programming language COBOL is completed.
IBM ship the transistor-based IBM 1401 mainframe.
Jersey Zoo (later Durrell Wildlife Park) established by Gerald Durrell.
Richard Feynman delivers a lecture "There's Plenty of Room at the Bottom", anticipating the field of nanotechnology.
Gordon Gould publishes the term Laser.
First known case of human HIV, in the Belgian Congo.
Agfa introduces the first fully automatic camera, the Optima.

Valdivia earthquake: Chile's subduction fault ruptures from Talcahuano to the Taitao Peninsula (with its epicenter near Lumaco), causing the most powerful earthquake on record (with a magnitude of 9.5) and a tsunami.
Robin Hill and Fay Bendall publish the 'Z scheme' of electron transport in photosynthesis.
11th General Conference on Weights and Measures establishes the International System of Units, abbreviated SI from the French name, Le Système international d'unités.
Edsger W. Dijkstra and Jaap A. Zonneveld produce the first (X1) implementation of the ALGOL 60 programming language.
At the Kasakela Chimpanzee Community, Jane Goodall observes a chimpanzee using a grass stalk to extract termites from a termite hill, the first recorded case of tool use by animals.
Climatron geodesic dome greenhouse opens at the Missouri Botanical Garden in St. Louis.
Arthur Leonard Schawlow and Charles Hard Townes receive the first patent for a laser.

The U.S. Food and Drug Administration announces that it will approve birth control as an additional indication for G. D. Searle's Enovid, making it the world's first approved combined oral contraceptive pill.
Jacques Piccard and Don Walsh reach bottom in the Mariana Trench in United States Navy bathyscaphe Trieste at a depth of 10,916 m.
Christopher Wagner and colleagues demonstrate a causal connection between exposure to crocidolite (fibrous riebeckite) (blue asbestos) and the lung cancer mesothelioma.
Apollo program: President Kennedy announces before a special joint session of Congress his goal to initiate a project to put a "man on the Moon" before the end of the decade.
Yuri Gagarin is the first human in space, making a single Low Earth orbit in Vostok 1 before parachuting to the ground.
Spain joins CERN; Yugoslavia leaves.
A Leadbeater's possum, a marsupial species thought to have been extinct for over 50 years, is discovered in New South Wales (Australia).
J. Heinrich Matthaei performs the Poly-U-Experiment in the United States, opening the way to solution of the genetic code, a key event in modern genetics.
Cephalosporin C is first characterized, by Guy Newton and Edward Abraham of the Sir William Dunn School of Pathology in the University of Oxford.
Discovery of the chemical elements: Element 103, Lawrencium, is first synthesized at Berkeley, California.

The non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drug Ibuprofen, derived from propanoic acid by the research arm of Boots UK (Andrew R. M. Dunlop with Stewart Adams, John Nicholson, Vonleigh Simmons, Jeff Wilson and Colin Burrows), is patented.
James L. Buie patents transistor-coupled transistor logic, later known as transistor-to-transistor logic circuitry (TTL), used in integrated circuits.
Ham, a 37-pound male chimpanzee, is rocketed into space in a test of the Project Mercury capsule designed to carry United States astronauts into space.
Nodding disease is first documented, in southern Tanzania.
The Canadian Alouette 1, the first satellite built outside the United States or the Soviet Union, is launched from Vandenberg Air Force Base in California.
J. C. R. Licklider begins to refer to the Intergalactic Computer Network, effectively conceptualizing what will become the Internet.
Simula I, the first object-oriented programming language, developed at the Norwegian Computing Center in Oslo by Ole-Johan Dahl and Kristen Nygaard, is released.
The first nude mouse strain is discovered by N. R. Grist at Ruchill Hospital's Brownlee virology laboratory in Glasgow.
3C 273, the first object to be identified as a quasar, is found by John Bolton with the radio telescope at the Parkes Observatory in New South Wales.
The earliest recorded use of the term "personal computer" features in The New York Times in a story about John Mauchly's speech the day before to the American Institute of Industrial Engineers.
Emile Zuckerkandl and Linus Pauling publish a paper introducing what will become known as the molecular clock concept.
Rachel Carson's Silent Spring begins serialization in The New Yorker; it is released as a book on September 27.
The "Hastings Rarities" are exposed as ornithological frauds.
The Icelandic volcanic island of Surtsey appears above sea level.
Mellotron Mark I electromechanical polyphonic tape replay keyboard, developed and built in Aston, Birmingham, England, is marketed.
Stanisław Ulam devises the Ulam spiral as a graphical depiction of the set of prime numbers.
David H. Frisch and J. H. Smith prove radioactive decay of mesons is slowed by their motion. (See Einstein's special relativity and general relativity.).
Molecular biologist Emile Zuckerkandl and physical chemist Linus Pauling introduce the term paleogenetics.
Ivan Sutherland writes the revolutionary Sketchpad program and runs it on the Lincoln TX-2 computer at Massachusetts Institute of Technology.
Don Buchla begins to design an electronic music synthesizer in Berkeley, California.

First definite identification of a radio source, 3C 48, with an optical object, later identified as a quasar, is published by Allan Sandage and Thomas A. Matthews; also Maarten Schmidt publishes significant observations on 3C 273.
First episode of science fiction television series Doctor Who broadcast by the BBC in the United Kingdom.
Guy Alexandre performs the first kidney transplantation from a heart-beating, brain-dead donor, at Saint Pierre Hospital, Leuven, Belgium.
Ranger program: Ranger 7 sends back the first close-up photographs of the Moon; images are 1,000 times clearer than anything ever seen from Earth-bound telescopes.
Jerome Horwitz synthesizes zidovudine (AZT), an antiviral drug that will come to be used in treating HIV.

The Soviet Union launches the Voskhod 1 into Earth orbit as the first spacecraft with a multi-person crew and the first flight without space suits (the crew wouldn't fit in the space capsule otherwise).
Great Alaskan earthquake, the second most powerful known, with a magnitude of 9.2.
British molecular biologist Robin Holliday proposes existence of the Holliday junction in nucleic acid.
Fernando Alves Martins of Portugal applies optical fiber technology to a gastrocamera to produce the first such device with a flexible fiberscope, for use in esophagogastroduodenoscopy.
Jacques Tits publishes significant work on group theory.
Spring – First recognition of cosmic microwave background radiation as a detectable phenomenon, securing the Big Bang as the best theory of the origin and evolution of the universe.
Existence of the charm quark is speculated by James Bjorken and Sheldon Glashow.
The Smithsonian Institution's Museum of History and Technology opens to the public in Washington, D.C.
CDC 6600 supercomputer delivered to CERN in Geneva.
Frank Pantridge installs the first portable defibrillator, in a Belfast ambulance.
At the Hammaguira launch facility in the Sahara Desert, France launches a Diamant-A rocket with its first satellite, Astérix-1 on board, becoming the third country to enter space.
The Parma wallaby, thought for around 70 years to be extinct, is rediscovered on Kawau Island (near Auckland).
Wang Yinglai and colleagues perform the first successful synthesis of insulin.
Emile Zuckerkandl and Linus Pauling name their concept of the molecular clock.
Ranger 8 crashes into the Moon after a successful mission of photographing possible landing sites for the Apollo program astronauts.
Mathematician Roger Penrose publishes a key paper on gravitational collapse and space-time singularities.
English paediatrician Harry Angelman first describes Angelman syndrome.
NASA launches Gemini 5 (Gordon Cooper, Pete Conrad) on the first 1-week space flight, as well as the first test of fuel cells for electrical power on such a mission.
The first live specimen of a mountain pygmy possum (Burramys parvus), Australia's only truly hibernating marsupial, previously known only from the fossil record, is discovered.
German entomologist Willi Hennig's Phylogenetic Systematics is published in English, advancing the study of cladistics.
Venera 3 Soviet space probe crashes on Venus becoming the first spacecraft to land on another planet's surface.
Notable display of the Leonids over the Americas.
Long-term potentiation (LTP), the putative cellular mechanism of learning and memory, is first observed by Terje Lømo in Oslo, Norway.
NASA spacecraft Gemini 8 (David Scott, Neil Armstrong) conducts the first docking in space, with an Agena target vehicle.
Martin Richards designs the BCPL programming language.
Chen Jingrun publishes Chen's theorem: every sufficiently large even number can be written as the sum of a prime and a semiprime.
Victor A. McKusick publishes the first edition of his catalogue of all known genes and genetic disorders, Mendelian Inheritance in Man.
First proposals for optical fiber communication presented by Charles K. Kao with George Hockham.
The United States, Soviet Union and UK sign the Outer Space Treaty.
Ole-Johan Dahl and Kristen Nygaard present their paper on Class and Subclass declarations at the IFIP Working Conference on simulation languages in Oslo.
First use, in a case of myocardial infarction, of the intra-aortic balloon pump invented by Dr Adrian Kantrowitz and his brother Arthur.

Ruth Sonntag Nussenzweig publishes her demonstration that mice can acquire immunity to the Plasmodium berghei parasite by exposing the mice to P. berghei sporozoites that have been inactivated by X-ray irradiation.
Dr Adrian Kantrowitz performs the first pediatric heart transplant, at Maimonides Medical Center in Brooklyn, United States, on a 19-day-old infant, who survives for six hours.
Apollo program: NASA launches a Saturn V rocket carrying the unmanned Apollo 4 test spacecraft from Cape Kennedy.
Errett Bishop publishes Foundations of Constructive Analysis, proving theorems in real analysis using constructive analysis.
The electroweak interaction theory is introduced by Steven Weinberg.
Chimpanzee Washoe begins to learn American Sign Language.
Astronauts Gus Grissom, Ed White, and Roger B. Chaffee are killed in a fire during a plugs-out test for Apollo 1.
Apollo program: NASA launches Apollo 7, the first crewed Apollo mission, with astronauts Wally Schirra, Donn Fulton Eisele and R. Walter Cunningham aboard.
Outbreak of acute gastroenteritis among schoolchildren in Norwalk, Ohio, caused by "Norwalk agent", the first identified norovirus.
The semiconductor chip company Intel is founded by Gordon E. Moore and Robert Noyce in Mountain View, California.
Thomas Gold explains the recently discovered radio pulsars as rapidly rotating neutron stars; subsequent observations confirm the suggestion.
Georges Charpak develops the multiwire proportional chamber for particle detection at CERN.
Dr. Christiaan Barnard performs the second successful human heart transplant, in South Africa, on Philip Blaiberg, who survives for nineteen months.
A human heart transplant performed at the Medical College of Virginia leads to a 4-year legal case, Tucker v. Lower, over the definition of brain death.
John Darley and Bibb Latané demonstrate the bystander effect.
The condition diffuse panbronchiolitis is named, in Japan.
A teenager known as 'Robert R.' dies in St. Louis, Missouri, of a baffling medical condition.
Last Przewalski's Horse sighted in the wild, in Mongolia.
Apollo program: Apollo 12 astronauts Charles Conrad and Alan Bean land at Oceanus Procellarum ("Ocean of Storms") and become the third and fourth humans to walk on the Moon.
Apollo program: 20:17 UTC – The human race, represented by Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin, lands on the Moon in the Apollo 11 Lunar Module Eagle.
Initial release of Multics ("Multiplexed Information and Computing Service"), an influential early time-sharing operating system based on the concept of a single-level memory.
Dorothy Hodgkin and colleagues at the University of Oxford determine the structure of insulin.
Apollo program: Apollo 9 returns safely to Earth after testing the Lunar Module.
Eugene, Oregon, has a record snowfall of 3 feet in 3 days: a pineapple express moves into the region with a shot of cold air, followed by some snow showers.
The B programming language is developed at Bell Labs by Ken Thompson and Dennis Ritchie.
The Parc naturel régional de Camargue is established in the south of France.
The Ohsumi satellite is launched, making Japan the fourth country to launch a satellite into orbit.
Drilling on the Kola Superdeep Borehole begins on the Kola Peninsula of Russia.
The first case of monkeypox in humans is identified in the Democratic Republic of the Congo.
Bomber by Len Deighton, the first novel written on a word processor (the IBM MT/ST), is published in England.
The Xerox PARC computer laboratory is opened in Palo Alto, California.
The Cleddau Bridge collapses during construction in Wales, killing four and leading to the introduction of new standards for box girder bridges in the United Kingdom.
The first United States patent for the computer mouse is issued to Douglas Engelbart.
The Explorer 1 satellite reenters the Earth's atmosphere after 12 years in orbit.
Venera 7 lands on Venus and becomes the first spacecraft to transmit data from another planet successfully (launched August 17).
Smallpox is eradicated from the Americas.
The Unix Programmer's Manual is published.
Kenbak-1 goes on sale, considered to be the world's first personal computer by the Computer History Museum and the American Computer Museum.
Apollo program: Apollo 14 returns to Earth after the third crewed Moon landing.
Intel release the world's first microprocessor, the 4004.

Michael S. Hart posts the first e-book, a copy of the United States Declaration of Independence, on the University of Illinois at Urbana–Champaign's mainframe computer, the origin of Project Gutenberg.
Ray Tomlinson sends the first ARPAnet e-mail between host computers, at BBN, Cambridge, Massachusetts, with the first use of the @ sign in an address.
E. G. L. Bywaters characterizes adult-onset Still's disease, a rare form of inflammatory arthritis.
Paris Descartes University begins to function in continuation of the medical department of the University of Paris.
Roger Penrose proposes the Penrose process.
A Blueprint for Survival first published as a special edition of The Ecologist magazine in the United Kingdom.
The First International Conference on Computer Communications is held in Washington, D.C., and hosts the first public demonstration of ARPAnet, a precursor of the Internet.
President of the United States Richard Nixon orders the development of a Space Shuttle program.
The last major epidemic of smallpox in Europe breaks out in Yugoslavia.
The International Time Bureau adds the first leap second to Coordinated Universal Time (UTC).
The United States launches Landsat 1, the first Earth-resources satellite.
Immunosuppressive effect of ciclosporin discovered by a team at Sandoz, Basel, under Hartmann F. Stähelin.
The first scientific hand-held calculator (labeled Hewlett-Packard, later designated the HP-35) is introduced, at a price of $395.00.
The Soviet uncrewed spacecraft Luna 20 lands on the Moon.
English inventor Peter Powell develops a steerable dual-line kite.
Asymmetric key algorithms for public-key cryptography developed by James H. Ellis, Clifford Cocks and Malcolm J. Williamson at the United Kingdom Government Communications Headquarters.
The first handheld mobile phone call is made by Martin Cooper of Motorola in New York City.
The American Psychiatric Association removes the definition of homosexuality as a mental disorder from the 2nd edition of its Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders (DSM-II).
Very long total solar eclipse visible in NE South America, the Atlantic, and central Africa.
Skylab, the United States' first space station, is launched.
Xerox PARC releases the Xerox Alto, the first computer designed to support an operating system based on a graphical user interface.
The term "Norrmalmstorgssyndromet", translated as Stockholm syndrome, is coined by Nils Bejerot.
Pioneer program: Pioneer 10 sends back the first close-up images of Jupiter.
Fischer Black and Myron Scholes first articulate the Black–Scholes mathematical model used in the financial field containing certain derivative investment instruments.
The term "dendritic cell" is coined by Ralph M. Steinman working with Zanvil A. Cohn.
"Smiling Buddha", India's first nuclear test explosion takes place underground at Pokhran.
Outbreak of 4-year Gombe Chimpanzee War in Tanzania, reported by Jane Goodall.

F. W. Winterbotham publishes The Ultra secret: the inside story of Operation Ultra, Bletchley Park and Enigma, the first popular account of cryptography carried out at Bletchley Park during World War II.
Identification of controlled trials in perinatal medicine, as advocated by Archie Cochrane, begins in Cardiff, Wales.
Hawking radiation is predicted by Stephen Hawking.
After 84 days in space, the last crew of the temporary American space station Skylab return to Earth.
Rubik's Cube invented by Ernő Rubik.
The Universal Product Code is scanned for the first time, to sell a package of Wrigley's chewing gum at the Marsh Supermarket in Troy, Ohio, the first use of barcode technology in American retailing.
The Mark-8 microcomputer based on the Intel 8008 microprocessor is designed by Jonathan Titus.
Yves Hellegouarch proposes a connection between Fermat's Last Theorem and the Frey curve.
Living specimens of the Chacoan Peccary (Catagonus wagneri), previously known only from fossils, are identified in Paraguay.
Bill Gates and Paul Allen form a company at this time called Micro-Soft in Albuquerque, New Mexico, to develop and sell their Altair BASIC interpreter software for the Altair 8800.
The last naturally occurring case of smallpox is diagnosed and treated, the victim being two-year-old Rahima Banu in Bangladesh.
The term global warming is probably first used in its modern sense by Wallace Smith Broecker.
The Monty Hall problem in probability is first posed, by Steve Selvin.
Apollo–Soyuz Test Project: An American Apollo and a Soviet Soyuz spacecraft dock with each other in orbit marking the first such link-up between spacecraft from the two nations.
Mini–mental state examination (MMSE) or Folstein test introduced to screen for dementia or other cognitive dysfunction.
Hackers in Silicon Valley hold the first meeting of the Homebrew Computer Club.
The MOS Technology 6502 is introduced.
Benoit Mandelbrot coins the term fractal.
The Ebola virus first emerges in outbreaks of viral hemorrhagic fever in Yambuku, Zaire, followed by outbreaks in Sudan.
Opening of the Dibner Library of the History of Science and Technology at the Smithsonian Institution's National Museum of History and Technology in Washington, D.C.
Apple Computer Company is formed by Steve Jobs and Steve Wozniak in California and on April 11 they launch their first computer, the Apple I, for the U.S. hobbyist market.
Gravity Probe A, a satellite-based experiment to test Albert Einstein's theory of general relativity, is launched.
Universe, a public domain film produced by Lester Novros for NASA, is released.
British evolutionary biologist Richard Dawkins' book The Selfish Gene is published, introducing the term memetics.
The four color theorem is proved by Kenneth Appel and Wolfgang Haken, the first major theorem to be proved using a computer.
First flight of production General Dynamics F-16 Fighting Falcon.
The Cray-1, the first commercially developed supercomputer, is released by Seymour Cray's Cray Research.
Release of Electric Pencil (originated by Michael Shrayer), the first word processor for home computers.
The world's last natural infection of smallpox is reported in Somalia.
Carl Woese and George E. Fox classify archaea as a new, separate domain of life.
Voyager program: Voyager 1 is launched after a brief delay.
Thorne–Żytkow objects, a bizarre hybrid of red supergiants and neutron stars, are first theorised.
Voyager program: The United States launches the Voyager 2 spacecraft to study the outer Solar System.
The first Apple II home computers (largely designed by Steve Wozniak) go on sale in the U.S., among the first successful mass-produced microcomputers.
Dr Raymond Damadian with Larry Minkoff and Michael Goldsmith perform the first magnetic resonance imaging body scan of a human.
The first complete genome is sequenced - a tiny bacterium-infecting virus called Phi X 174, with just 11 genes, and a little over 5000 base pairs.
Frederick Sanger and colleagues introduce Sanger sequencing.
Steven Weinberg publishes the first edition of The First Three Minutes: A Modern View of the Origin of the Universe in the United States.
James Burke's history of science series Connections first airs, on BBC Television in the United Kingdom (with accompanying book).
The first computer bulletin board system is created (CBBS in Chicago, Illinois).
Victor Skumin first describes "cardioprosthetic psychopathological syndrome", later known as "Skumin syndrome", a form of anxiety suffered by recipients of artificial heart valves.
James W. Christy at the United States Naval Observatory discovers Charon, the first moon of Pluto identified.
Louise Brown becomes the world's first human born from in vitro fertilisation, in England.
The rare genetic disorder Pitt–Hopkins syndrome is first described.
The RSA algorithm for public-key cryptography, based on the factoring problem, is first publicly described by Ron Rivest, Adi Shamir and Leonard Adleman.
First stage of Kakadu National Park declared in Australia.
The RISE project first discovers hydrothermal vents known as 'black smokers', on a mid-ocean ridge in the Pacific Ocean.
Pluto enters a 20-year period inside the orbit of Neptune for the first time in 230 years.
May 8 - Radio Shack releases TRSDOS 2.3.
The World Health Organization certifies the global eradication of smallpox.

Human-powered aircraft Gossamer Albatross, built by an American team led by Paul MacCready and piloted by Bryan Allen, makes a successful crossing of the English Channel to win the second Kremer prize.
The last naturally occurring cases of polio are reported in the United States.
Philips publicly demonstrate a prototype of an optical digital audio disc at a press conference in Eindhoven, Netherlands.
The first modern Sudoku, known as Number Place, appears in Dell Pencil Puzzles and Word Games (United States), devised by Howard Garns.

America's first space station, Skylab, is deliberately allowed to burn up on atmospheric entry over the Indian Ocean due to its decaying orbit and the lack of time to build a new spaceship to boost it up.
First commercial MRI whole body scanner manufactured by Oxford Instruments for installation at Hammersmith Hospital, London.
Global eradication of smallpox certified by the World Health Organization.
Microsoft's Bill Gates agrees to create an operating system for the new IBM Personal Computer.
Tim Berners-Lee begins work on ENQUIRE, the system that will lead to the creation of the World Wide Web a decade later.
The Cooloola monster, an orthopteran, is discovered in Queensland, Australia.

John B. Goodenough, working with colleagues at the University of Oxford Inorganic Chemistry Laboratory, identifies the cathode material that enables development of the rechargeable lithium-ion battery.
Global Positioning System time epoch begins at 00:00 UTC.
The Voyager 1 probe confirms the existence of Janus, a moon of Saturn.
Digital Equipment Corporation, Intel and Xerox introduce the DIX standard for Ethernet, which is the first implementation outside of Xerox and the first to support 10 Mbit/s speeds.

First clinically useful image of a patient's internal tissues using magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) is obtained using a full-body scanner built by a team led by John Mallard at the University of Aberdeen.
Pantanal Matogrossense National Park designated in Brazil.
AIDS pandemic begins when the United States Centers for Disease Control and Prevention reports an unusual cluster of Pneumocystis pneumonia in five homosexual men in Los Angeles.
The Osborne 1, the first successful portable computer, is unveiled at the West Coast Computer Faire in San Francisco.
Nintendo releases the arcade game Donkey Kong featuring the debut of Mario.
Hyatt Regency walkway collapse: Structural failure due to a late design change causes two internal suspended walkways at the Hyatt Regency Hotel in Kansas City, Missouri to collapse, killing 114.
The first launch of a Space Shuttle: Columbia launches on the STS-1 mission.
English psychiatrist Lorna Wing introduces the term "Asperger syndrome".
UoSAT-1, the first modern microsatellite, is launched into Low Earth orbit.
Publication of Stephen Jay Gould's critique of biological determinism, The Mismeasure of Man, in the United States.
The IBM Personal Computer is released.
Syzygy: all 9 planets align on the same side of the Sun.
Allen Hill and colleagues at the University of Oxford develop a glucose biosensor.
Helen House, the world’s first children’s hospice, is set up by Sister Frances Dominica in Oxford, England.
First computer virus, the Elk Cloner, written by 15-year-old Rich Skrenta, is found in the wild.
Halley's Comet: First spotted in the sky after 70 year return.
Night Thoughts of a Classical Physicist is published by Russell McCormmach.

Allan Hills A81005, the first lunar meteorite found on Earth, is discovered in the Allan Hills at the end of the Transantarctic Mountains by John Schutt and Ian Whillans during the ANSMET meteorite gathering expedition.
Sci-fi movie Tron is the first feature film to use computer animation extensively.
The Commodore 64 8-bit home computer is launched by Commodore International (released in August); it becomes the all-time best-selling single personal computer model.
At the University of Utah, 61-year-old retired dentist Barney Clark becomes the first person to receive a permanent artificial heart; he lives for 112 days with the device.
Pioneer 10 passes the orbit of Neptune, becoming the first man-made object to travel beyond the major planets of the Solar System.
World's first dedicated hospital ward for HIV/AIDS patients opens at San Francisco General Hospital.
At the seventeenth General Conference on Weights and Measures, the length of a metre is redefined as the distance light travels in vacuum in 1/299,792,458 of a second.
First reports of HIV as a possible cause of AIDS, by independent virology teams led by Luc Montagnier and Robert Gallo.
Richard Stallman announces the GNU Project.
Fred Cohen demonstrates a self-replicating source code which his academic adviser at the University of Southern California, Leonard Adleman, likens to a virus.
The Soyuz T-10-1 mission ends in a pad abort at the Baikonur Cosmodrome, when a pad fire occurs at the base of the Soyuz U rocket during the launch countdown.
Word processor software Multi-Tool Word, soon to become Microsoft Word, is released.
The ARPANET officially changes to use the Internet Protocol, creating the Internet.
Kary Mullis discovers polymerase chain reaction.
First known case of Bovine spongiform encephalopathy, in England.
The enzyme telomerase is discovered by Carol W. Greider and Elizabeth Blackburn in the ciliate Tetrahymena.
In Jackson, Michigan, a factory robot crushes a worker against a safety bar in apparently the first robot-related death in the United States.
Dr Robert Gallo and Margaret Heckler of United States Public Health Service announce the discovery of HTLV-III as the virus that causes AIDS.
Apple Computer places the Macintosh personal computer on sale in the United States.
Itaipu Dam in South America begins to generate hydroelectricity.
Peter Kramer and Dan Shechtman publish their discoveries of what will soon afterwards be named quasicrystals.
Barbara H. Bowman and Oliver Smithies show that variations in haptoglobins are due to genetic polymorphisms.
Seasonal affective disorder is formally described and named by Norman E. Rosenthal MD and colleagues in the United States as a mood disorder.
Astronauts Bruce McCandless II and Robert L. Stewart make the first untethered space walk.
The first commercial Internet domain name, in the top-level domain .com, is registered in the name symbolics.com by Symbolics Inc., a computer systems firm in Cambridge, Massachusetts.
Microsoft Windows operating system released.
The first British mobile phone calls are made.
The GNU Manifesto, written by Richard Stallman, is first published.
Physicist Carl Sagan's hard science fiction novel Contact is published in the United States, introducing the concept of a traversable wormhole devised by Kip Thorne.
Jean-Pierre Serre provides partial proof that a Frey curve cannot be modular, showing that a proof of the semistable case of the Taniyama-Shimura conjecture would imply Fermat's Last Theorem.
Scientists of the British Antarctic Survey announce discovery of the ozone hole.
Akira Yoshino develops a practical lithium-ion battery.
Minolta releases the Maxxum 7000, the world's first autofocus single-lens reflex camera.
New York-based neurologist Oliver Sacks publishes The Man Who Mistook His Wife for a Hat and Other Clinical Tales.
NASA Voyager 2 space probe makes first encounter with Uranus.

Rutan Voyager becomes the first aircraft to fly around the world without stopping or refueling, landing at Edwards Air Force Base in California after a nine-day trip piloted by Dick Rutan and Jeana Yeager.
The Gateway Bridge is opened in Brisbane, Australia, the world's largest prestressed concrete single box bridge.
Chernobyl disaster: An RBMK at Chernobyl Nuclear Power Plant in the Ukrainian Soviet Socialist Republic reaches prompt criticality.
The first MS-DOS-based personal computer virus, Brain, starts to spread.
Japanese spacecraft Suisei flies by Halley's Comet, studying its UV hydrogen corona and solar wind.
The Soviet Union launches the Mir space station.
NASA Space Shuttle Challenger explodes on launch, killing all seven astronauts aboard.

Summer – Kenneth Alan Ribet demonstrates proof of the ε-conjecture, subsequently known as Ribet's theorem confirming Gerhard Frey's suggestion that the Taniyama–Shimura conjecture implies Fermat's Last Theorem.
3D printing is developed by Charles Hull.
The United States Food and Drug Administration for the first time approves an antiretroviral drug for the treatment of HIV/AIDS, zidovudine, also known as AZT (azidothymidine) or Retrovir.
HyperCard is released by Apple Inc., an early example of hypermedia which inspires the World Wide Web.
Larry Wall releases the first version of the Perl programming language via the comp.sources.misc newsgroup.
Florida rapist Tommie Lee Andrews is the first person to be convicted as a result of DNA fingerprinting.
The Abelian sandpile model, the first discovered example of a dynamical system displaying self-organized criticality, is published by Per Bak, Chao Tang and Kurt Wiesenfeld.
The 'Mitochondrial Eve' hypothesis is proposed.
The FDA for the first time approves a statin, lovastatin.
Yoshizumi Ishino discovers the DNA sequence of CRISPR.
September 5 - The first successful surgical separation of craniopagus twins is done by Dr. Ben Carson.
Internet Relay Chat, the first Internet-based chat protocol, is created by Jarkko Oikarinen in Finland.
Tim Berners-Lee begins openly to discuss his plans for what will become the World Wide Web at CERN.
NASA climate scientist James Hansen uses the term global warming in testimony to the United States Congress bringing it to public attention.
2nd International Studies of Infarct Survival (ISIS-2) demonstrates beneficial effects of aspirin in treatment of myocardial infarction.
In the Soviet Union, the uncrewed Shuttle Buran is launched by an Energia rocket on her maiden orbital spaceflight (this was the first and last space flight for the shuttle).
The Morris worm, the first computer worm distributed via the Internet, written by Robert Tappan Morris, is launched from Massachusetts Institute of Technology in the U.S.
NASA resumes Space Shuttle flights, grounded after the Challenger disaster.
Patricia Bath patents the Laserphaco Probe, a device "for ablating and removing cataract lenses".
TAT-8, the first transatlantic telephone cable to use optical fiber, is completed, facilitating linking of the American and European Internet.
The first version of the Photoshop graphics software, devised by Thomas Knoll, ships with Barneyscan image scanners.
The Voyager 2 spacecraft makes its closest approach to Neptune, providing definitive proof of the planet's rings.
Tim Berners-Lee submits a memorandum, titled "Information Management: A Proposal", to the management at CERN for a system that would eventually become the World Wide Web.
Cosmic Background Explorer launched, "the starting point for cosmology as a precision science".
Pluto–Charon barycentre comes to perihelion.
Isamu Akasaki produces the first Gallium nitride p-n junction blue/UV light-emitting diode.
The New Zealand Department of Conservation begins to implement a Kākāpō Recovery Plan.
The Northrop Grumman B-2 Spirit "Stealth Bomber" aircraft, developed for the United States Air Force, first flies.
Discovery of the cystic fibrosis trans-membrane conductance regulator gene.
Stanley Pons and Martin Fleischmann announce cold fusion at the University of Utah.
The first known web page is written.
Satoshi Tajiri begins creating the first Pokémon game.
The Pale Blue Dot photograph of Earth is sent back from the Voyager 1 probe after completing its primary mission, from around 3.5 billion miles away.

The first evidence for the existence of the BRCA gene encoding for a DNA repair enzyme involved in breast cancer susceptibility Is provided by Mary-Claire King's laboratory at University of California, Berkeley.
Adobe Photoshop 1.0 graphics software, devised by Thomas Knoll, is released.
The Space Shuttle Discovery places the Hubble Space Telescope into orbit.
The Human Genome Project is founded.
May 22 - Windows 3.0 is shipped by Microsoft.
Linus Torvalds posts messages to the Usenet newsgroup comp.os.minix, regarding the new operating system kernel he has developed, called Linux.
Apple releases the PowerBook laptop computer.
Python, a programming language created by Guido van Rossum, Is released.
The first website goes online at CERN.
The video game Sonic the Hedgehog is first released, propelling the Sega Genesis 16-bit console into mass popularity.
There are two solar eclipses: one annular eclipse on January 15, and a very long total eclipse on July 11 (lasting 6 minutes and 53 seconds).
Tim Berners-Lee, an English computer scientist working at CERN, introduces WorldWideWeb (the first web browser), and a WYSIWYG HTML editor.
There are four lunar eclipses: three penumbral on January 30, July 26, and June 27, and one minor partial lunar eclipse on December 21.
Phil Zimmermann posts the first Pretty Good Privacy (PGP) data encryption program.
World's first GSM telephone call made in Finland.
Saola first identified in the Vũ Quang rainforest reserve of northern Vietnam.
Pope John Paul II issues an apology and lifts the 1633 edict of the Inquisition against Galileo Galilei.
The IBM Simon, a touchscreen mobile phone and personal digital assistant considered the first smartphone, is introduced.
ViolaWWW, the first popular Web browser, created by Pei-Yuan Wei in the United States, is publicly released for Unix.

First confirmed detection of exoplanets with announcement of the discovery of several terrestrial-mass planets orbiting the pulsar PSR B1257+12 by radio astronomers Aleksander Wolszczan and Dale Frail working in the United States.
Discovery of 15760 Albion, the first trans-Neptunian object to be found after Pluto and Charon.

British anthropologist Robin Dunbar proposes Dunbar's number (approximately 150) as a cognitive limit to the number of people with whom an interpersonal relationship can be maintained in human communities.
Czech Republic and Slovakia join CERN.
Release of version 1.0 of the Mosaic Web browser, devised by Marc Andreessen and Eric Bina in the United States.
Adobe publishes the first version of the PDF format together with version 1.0 of its PDF product line Adobe Acrobat.
The Intel Corporation ships the first Pentium chips.
A study published by Dean Hamer and others in the United States indicates a link between the chromosome band and genetic marker Xq28 and male sexual orientation.
The "Intelligent Prosthesis", the first commercially available microprocessor-controlled prosthetic knee, is released by UK company Charles A. Blatchford & Sons.
Andrew Wiles announces a proof of Fermat's Last Theorem at the Isaac Newton Institute.
A bug in a program written by Richard Depew sends an article to 200 newsgroups simultaneously.
Leon M. Lederman and Dick Teresi publish The God Particle.
The first definite asteroid moon is confirmed when the Galileo probe discovers Dactyl orbiting 243 Ida.
Sony release the PlayStation fifth generation home video game console in Japan.
Darmstadtium first detected at the Gesellschaft für Schwerionenforschung (GSI) in Darmstadt, Germany, by Peter Armbruster and Gottfried Münzenberg, under the direction of Prof.
The first three atoms of Roentgenium are observed by an international team led by Sigurd Hofmann at the GSI in Darmstadt.
Apple Computer, Inc. releases the Power Macintosh, the first Macintosh computers to use the new PowerPC microprocessors.
Jerry Yang and David Filo create "Jerry's Guide to the World Wide Web", a hierarchically organised website, while studying at Stanford University; in April it is renamed Yahoo!.
Netscape launch the Netscape Navigator web browser, for which it creates HTTP Secure.
Wollemia (the 'Wollemi Pine'), previously known only from fossils, is discovered living in remote rainforest gorges in the Wollemi National Park of New South Wales by David Noble.

Leonard Adleman describes the experimental use of DNA as a computational system to solve a seven-node instance of the Hamiltonian path problem, the first known instance of the successful use of DNA to compute an algorithm.
The first gene linked to Alzheimer's disease is discovered.
The BRCA1 gene is cloned by scientists at University of Utah, National Institute of Environmental Health Sciences (NIEHS) and Myriad Genetics.
The first SampTA conference for mathematicians, engineers and applied scientists is held in Riga, Latvia.
Sudden oak death, the tree disease caused by the plant pathogen Phytophthora ramorum, is first observed, in California, United States.
The United States government stops funding the NSFNET, making the Internet a wholly privatized system.
Danish/Greenlandic/Canadian programmer Rasmus Lerdorf releases the first version of the scripting language PHP, which in 15 years will be used as the server-side language on 75% of all Web servers.
Ward Cunningham loads the first wiki software, WikiWikiWeb, in Oregon.
Prodigy (online service) offers access to the World Wide Web.
Project Phoenix begins looking for extraterrestrial transmissions using the Parkes Observatory radio telescope in New South Wales, Australia, the largest telescope in the Southern Hemisphere.
Cosmonaut Valeri Polyakov returns after setting a record for 438 days in space.
The Java programming language is announced to the world.
Toy Story, the first feature film created using only computer-generated imagery, is released in theaters in the United States.
The Google web search engine originates as "BackRub", a research project using PageRank by Larry Page and Sergey Brin, PhD students at Stanford University, California.
Dolly the sheep, the first mammal to be successfully cloned from an adult cell, is born at The Roslin Institute in Scotland.
Swede Göran Kropp reaches Mount Everest summit alone without oxygen after having bicycled there from Sweden.
Deep Blue defeats chess grand-master Garry Kasparov for the first time.
The role of CCR5 in HIV/AIDS infection begins to be published.
Reinhard Genzel and Andrea Ghez demonstrate the existence of a supermassive compact object at the centre of our galaxy, later identified as a black hole.
Montreal Cognitive Assessment is created by Ziad Nasreddine in Montreal, Quebec.
Severe thunderstorms and a tornado in Bangladesh kills at least 443 people.
Brewster Kahle, with Bruce Gilliat, develops the Wayback Machine software to crawl and archive World Wide Web pages.
The Shetland Times and The Shetland News become involved in a landmark legal case over alleged copyright infringement and deep linking in their websites.
IBM's Deep Blue defeats Garry Kasparov, the first time a computer defeats a chess grand master in a match.
High Resolution Fly's Eye Cosmic Ray Detector (HiRes) is built and operated on the Dugway Proving Grounds in the western Utah desert.
The domain name for the web search engine Google is registered.
Steve Jobs returns to Apple Inc. as a consultant after the company purchases his software startup NeXT.
United States President Bill Clinton bars federal funding for any research on human cloning.
"Lisa the Skeptic" first broadcast as an episode of The Simpsons in the United States.
GRB 970228, a highly luminous flash of gamma rays, strikes the Earth for 80 seconds, providing early evidence that gamma-ray bursts occur well beyond the Milky Way.
In London, scientists report their DNA analysis findings from a Neandertal skeleton which support the out of Africa theory of human evolution placing an "African Eve" at 100,000 to 200,000 years ago.
First test flight of the Lockheed Martin F-22 Raptor fifth-generation jet fighter.
Launch of 10-year Cassini–Huygens spacecraft to Saturn.
The CIH virus is discovered in Taiwan.
Argentinian physicist Juan Maldacena publishes a landmark paper initiating the study of AdS/CFT correspondence, which links string theory and quantum gravity.
Google, Inc. is founded in Menlo Park, California, by Stanford University PhD candidates Larry Page and Sergey Brin to promote their web search engine.
Edinburgh Modular Arm System, the world's first bionic arm, is fitted.
Researchers in Dallas, Texas, present findings about an enzyme that slows aging and cell death (apoptosis).
Zarya, the first module of the International Space Station, is launched.
Biologists report in the journal Science how they sequenced the genome of the bacterium that causes syphilis, Treponema pallidum.
RNA interference first elucidated in the nematode Caenorhabditis elegans.
In Japan, the Akashi Kaikyō Bridge linking Shikoku with Honshū, at a cost of about US$3.8 billion, opens to traffic, becoming the longest-span suspension bridge in the world.
Data sent from the Galileo space probe indicates that Jupiter's moon Europa has a liquid ocean under a thick crust of ice.
A 6.0 Richter scale earthquake hits western Colombia, killing at least 1,000.
The bacterium Thiomargarita namibiensis is discovered off the coast of Namibia.
Stardust is launched on a mission to collect samples of a comet coma, and return them to Earth.
Late – Pest-exclusion fence around Zealandia (wildlife sanctuary) in Wellington, New Zealand, completed.
Elements 118 and 116 are claimed to be made for the first time; later retracted when results cannot be replicated.
David Bowie's Hours becomes the first complete music album by a major artist available to download over the Internet in advance of the physical release.
The Dunning–Kruger effect, a cognitive bias, is first described by American psychologists David Dunning and Justin Kruger.
The term 'Web 2.0' is coined by Darcy DiNucci.
The first BlackBerry is released, using the same hardware as the Inter@ctive pager 950, and running on the Mobitex network.
While trying to circumnavigate the world in a hot air balloon, Colin Prescot and Andy Elson set a new endurance record after being in their balloon for 233 hours and 55 minutes.
After originating in the Philippines, the ILOVEYOU computer virus spreads quickly throughout the world.
'First draft' of the Human Genome Project is announced jointly by President of the United States Bill Clinton and British Prime Minister Tony Blair.
Museu de les Ciències Príncipe Felipe in Valencia, Spain, opens to the public.
Expedition 1 to the International Space Station begins.
Stephen King's horror story Riding the Bullet is published in e-book format only, the world's first mass-market electronic book.

First system enabling the selection, automatic downloading and storage of serial episodic audio content on PCs and portable devices, origin of the podcast, is launched by early MP3 player manufacturer i2Go.
The Confederate States of America submarine H. L. Hunley is raised to the surface after 136 years on the ocean floor.
Sony Computer Entertainment releases the PlayStation 2 sixth generation home video game console in Japan.
Bastille Day solar storm: A powerful solar flare causes a geomagnetic storm on Earth.
The full genome sequence of the flowering plant Arabidopsis thaliana is published in Nature.
The Hubble Space Telescope detects sodium in the atmosphere of HD 209458 b, the first exoplanet atmosphere to be measured.
Windows XP personal computer operating system released by Microsoft; it is available for retail sale on October 25.
Apple Inc. releases the iTunes media player (modified from SoundJam MP).
Tim Berners-Lee and colleagues name the Semantic Web.
Craig Venter and Mark Adams complete the genetic map of the laboratory mouse.
Fossil remains of the whale Rodhocetus balochistanensis found in Balochistan province, Pakistan, by Philip D. Gingerich.
The first animal from an endangered species produced by cloning, a gaur named Noah, is born at Trans Ova Genetics in Sioux Center, Iowa.
The NEAR Shoemaker spacecraft lands in the "saddle" region of 433 Eros, becoming the first spacecraft to land on an asteroid.
NASA's Galileo spacecraft passes within 112 miles (180 km) of Jupiter's moon Io.
Francisco-Miguel Marqués and co-workers at the Grand Accélérateur National d'Ions Lourds in Caen claim to detect a tetraneutron; reproducibility of this observation has not been possible.
Eruption of Mount Nyiragongo in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, displacing an estimated 400,000 people.
New suborder of insects, Mantophasmatidae, announced.
DNA barcoding of the dodo is published, confirming it as a member of the Columbidae family.
Red wine is claimed by Spanish researchers to protect against the common cold.
The first version of the web browser Firefox is released by the Mozilla Organization.
The ringed dwarf planet Quaoar is discovered by astronomers Chad Trujillo and Michael Brown at the Palomar Observatory.
The Danger Hiptop is released, the first smartphone to incorporate instant messaging.
Severe acute respiratory syndrome (SARS) epidemic begins in Guangdong province of China.
The gene BRAF is shown to be faulty (mutated) in some human cancers.
The iMac G4 is introduced by Apple, Inc., as the next generation iMac.
November – The Sun is at solar maximum with a period of high activity, generating many large solar flares and coronal mass ejections.
Annular solar eclipse in Northern Scotland, Faroe Islands, Greenland, and Iceland, with partial eclipse covering much of Europe and Russia.
Discovery of Uranus's irregular moon Margaret (the only one with prograde motion) by Scott S. Sheppard and David C. Jewitt at Mauna Kea Observatory in Hawaii.
Space Shuttle Columbia disintegrates over Texas upon reentry killing all seven astronauts on board.
NASA's WMAP satellite completes the first detailed cosmic microwave background radiation map of the universe.
An American businessman is diagnosed with the first known case of SARS in Hanoi, Vietnam, by WHO doctor Carlo Urbani.
The 2dF Survey of galaxy redshifts is published.
A banteng delivered in the United States is the second successful cloning of an endangered species and the first such clone to survive beyond infancy.
The first European Mars mission Mars Express launched.
Intel releases the Pentium M microprocessor.
Remains of a previously unknown species of human is discovered in Indonesia.
Facebook launches: Mark Zuckerberg launches "TheFacebook" as a social networking website for Harvard University students.
Trees have a theoretical maximum height of 130 m (426 ft) before gravity restricts their growth, according to a study published in Nature.
A team from Australia, Russia and Greece announce a new material, made from a nano-foam of carbon that has the lowest density ever reported for a solid.
Scientists using the Chandra X-ray Observatory announced their findings that supports the notion that the expansion of the Universe is accelerating.

A flare of radiation from an explosion on the super-magnetic neutron star (Magnetar) SGR 1806-20 reaches Earth – astronomers later calculate that it is the largest explosion observed in the Milky Way galaxy for 400 years.
NASA's Stardust space probe flies by comet 81P/Wild and collects particle samples from its coma.
Astronomers from the European Southern Observatory (ESO) announce images that appear to show a planet orbiting a brown dwarf about 230 light-years away.
Scientists from the University of California, Irvine announce the first high-speed transistor made from a carbon nanotube, operating at microwave frequencies.
Russian and American physicists produce results that indicate the discovery of elements 113 and 115.
Two independent teams report the observation of light from planets circling two different stars, using the Spitzer infrared space telescope.
The first video is uploaded to the online video hosting service YouTube established by Jawed Karim, Steve Chen and Chad Hurley.
The Deep Impact spacecraft successfully observes the disintegration of its "impactor" section colliding with the comet Tempel 1. A large number of other telescopes also provide data on this event.
Dwarf planet Makemake is discovered in the Kuiper belt (discovery announced July 29).
The Huygens probe is successfully sent into the atmosphere of Titan and returns science data to Earth via the Cassini orbiter.
Yale University wins more than $1 million in damages and attorney's fees, along with the patent rights relating to electrospray ionization from former professor and Nobel Prize winner John Fenn.
The Spanish flu virus is reconstructed and shown to be closely related to the Avian influenza virus.
Astronomers announce the discovery of a galaxy, VIRGOHI21, that consists almost entirely of dark matter.
A first draft of the chimpanzee genome is published.
Michael Kosfeld and colleagues publish their findings that oxytocin increases trust in humans.
Total solar eclipse (Brazil, Greece, Mid Atlantic Ocean, Sahara, Turkey, Georgia, Russia, Kazakhstan, Mongolia).
Nontherian mammal fossils are identified among the St Bathans Fauna of New Zealand's South Island.
The Stardust spacecraft successfully completes its primary mission of returning samples of cometary and interstellar dust to Earth.
NASA's Stardust mission successfully ends, the first to return dust from a comet.
Baiji (Yangtze river dolphin) declared "functionally extinct".
Australian researchers at the CSIRO Marine and Atmospheric Research centre in Hobart, Tasmania, publish experimental data that matches models of increasing sea level rising.
Annular solar eclipse in South America, West Africa and Antarctica.
The discovery of nine additional natural satellites of Saturn published.
The construction of the International Space Station is continued for the first time after a hiatus of almost four years.
The sequence of the last chromosome in the Human Genome Project is published in the journal Nature.
4 March – A total lunar eclipse occurs, visible in some parts of the Americas and Asia, and in all of Europe and Africa.
Apple Inc.'s first iPhone smartphone is announced by Steve Jobs at Macworld in San Francisco; it is released in the United States on 29 June.
